title: The Evening Brief: Courts block Trump moves; primaries narrow the field
dek: Federal judges blocked the Trump administration's FBI headquarters relocation and preserved an earlier ruling against Trump in a defamation case. Disney sued the FCC over broadcast licenses, Minnesota sued Texas over an ICE agent's extradition, and primary elections clarified November matchups in Florida and Alaska.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: A series of judicial decisions constrained executive and regulatory action today, while primary elections in Florida and Alaska narrowed the field for November races in two strategically important states.
bottom_line: Federal courts constrained executive action on three separate fronts today: the FBI relocation on statutory grounds, the FCC's broadcast licensing order on First Amendment grounds (via Disney's suit), and an extradition dispute on interstate law. Primary elections in Florida and Alaska clarified November matchups in two strategically important states. Watch for the Trump administration's response to the Maryland FBI ruling, whether it appeals or seeks congressional action; the federal judge's decision on Disney's request for a temporary restraining order; and the scope and timeline of Israel's criminal investigation into Hind Rajab's death.
body: Three federal courts acted today to limit Trump administration authority. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang blocked the Trump administration from moving FBI headquarters from a planned site in Greenbelt, Maryland, to the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington, finding the decision exceeded statutory authority and violated federal law. The ruling prevents the administration from repurposing funds Congress had allocated for the Maryland project. A separate legal front opened when Disney and ABC sued the FCC on August 18, 2026, alleging the Trump administration orchestrated a retaliatory regulatory action requiring early license renewal of eight Disney-owned television stations, years ahead of schedule. Disney's legal team, including prominent attorneys Beth Wilkinson and Paul Clement, called the directive "unprecedented" and raised First Amendment questions about regulatory pressure on press freedom. The FCC disputes the retaliation claim, citing ongoing investigations into Disney's diversity practices and "The View" program's compliance with public interest standards.

A third dispute involved state-to-state conflict over federal law enforcement. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a federal lawsuit against Texas Governor Greg Abbott to compel the extradition of ICE agent Christian Castro, charged with assault with a deadly weapon and falsely reporting a crime. Castro was arrested in Texas in May after allegedly shooting a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis on January 14. The suit tests whether a sitting governor can legally refuse to return a federal agent for trial in another state.

Primary elections reshaped two major races heading into November. In Florida, Rep. Byron Donalds won the Republican gubernatorial primary and will face former Rep. David Jolly, who won the Democratic primary, in the general election to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has been backed by President Trump and is a prominent member of the House Freedom Caucus. In Florida's U.S. Senate race, Angie Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, defeated well-funded former National Security Council aide Alex Vindman in the Democratic primary. Nixon raised less than $1 million while Vindman, recruited by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, raised more than $16 million. She will face Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in November for the final two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio's term.

In Alaska, Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola both advanced to the November general election from the state's primary. A federal grand jury investigation into a same-named Republican candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, a former teacher, remains open. The investigation is examining whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. Alaska's November election will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

On the international front, the Israeli military confirmed for the first time that it fired on a car carrying five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in Gaza in 2024, reversing earlier denials. Israel announced a criminal investigation into her death and the killings of six relatives, two paramedics, and 15 others in a March 2025 incident. Rajab initially survived the attack and called for help during a hours-long phone call before the ambulance sent to retrieve her was shelled, killing the two paramedics. The Hind Rajab Foundation expressed no confidence in the investigation.
